newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African banks clip rates as shortage hits yr low.
newsitem.headline: S.African banks clip rates as shortage hits yr low.

text.p: South African commercial banks clipped their short-term deposit rates on Monday after the shortage fell to its lowest level since June 1996 at the weekend.

Three of South Africa's "big four" commercial banks quoted their three-month NCDs at 16.00 percent offered, from 16.05 percent on Friday, after the Reserve Bank said the shortage fell to 5.389 billion rand on Saturday -- its lowest level since June 28 last year.

Roelf du Plooy, assistant general manager of the Reserve Bank's money and capital market division, said the shortage had fallen as a result of a 400 million rand decline in notes and coins, a mismatch in government flows as well as an effort to cater for coupon flows in August.

"We decided to transfer some money from the exchequer account to the Tax and Loan accounts at the banks in order for the government to earn interest on the money and to build up balances ahead of the huge coupon payments in August," he said.

In August, coupons of about eight billion rand have to be paid on a number of government stocks, notably the R150 and R153. "We have to build up the balances gradually from now onwards to handle those large payments," Du Plooy said.
Du Plooy said that in the period leading up to July 1, when foreign exchange controls are liberalised, and thereafter, he expected the shortage to fluctuate between five and seven billion rand.
"The uncertain factor is July 1. If we receive a lot of foreign inflows at this stage, the Reserve Bank is going to buy up reserves and the shortage will decline further.
"But July 1 is just around the corner and if a lot of money leaves the country then the shortage will go up again," Du Plooy said.
"It is difficult to say what level it (the shortage) will hold, but up to the end of this month, I don't think the shortage will increase dramatically," he added.
Traders said that while the market was more comfortable with the shortage at its current level, a sustained lower shortage was needed for rates to move lower.
